title: Pipelined RISC-V Processor
text:
Introduction
For the 2026 System-on-Chip Design (E154) final project, my partner Max Conine and I turned a single-cycle RISC-V processor into a pipelined one. We then optimized it by shortening the critical path, reducing hazard penalties, and cutting area. The final processor scored over ten times the original’s figure of merit and ran CoreMark 62.4% faster.
The project gave us experience with the full SoC development loop: microarchitecture design, RTL in SystemVerilog, verification against compliance tests and benchmarks, and iterating on synthesis results.
The full project report and final presentation are available as PDFs.

title: Pipelined RISC-V Processor
text:
Microarchitecture
The processor uses a 5-stage pipeline implementing the RV32IM instruction set, with a dedicated 3-stage multiply unit and a hazard unit that handles forwarding, stalls, and flushes. The design is based on the pipelined processor from Digital Design and Computer Architecture, RISC-V Edition by David and Sarah Harris, and on the CORE-V Wally RISC-V processor.






Figure 1: Top-level block diagram of the 5-stage pipelined processor. The highlighted path through the instruction ROM is the critical path.




Implemented Extensions
RV32I. The base 32-bit integer instruction set provides everything a general-purpose computer needs:

Integer arithmetic: ADD, SUB, AND, OR, XOR, and shifts
Loads and stores of bytes, halfwords, and words
Conditional branches (BEQ, BNE, BLT, BGE, BLTU, BGEU) and jumps (JAL, JALR)
Set-less-than (SLT, SLTU)
Immediate operations (ADDI, ANDI, etc.)

Zmmul. The multiplication subset of the M extension, without division or remainder:

MUL: lower 32 bits of the product
MULH: upper 32 bits, signed × signed
MULHSU: upper 32 bits, signed × unsigned
MULHU: upper 32 bits, unsigned × unsigned

Hardware multiplication removes the software loops that RV32I would otherwise need, which cuts the number of instructions considerably.
Zicsr and Zicntr. These let software read the cycle and instructions-retired counters in the control and status register (CSR) file, which CoreMark uses to compute its score.

title: Pipelined RISC-V Processor
text:
Figure of Merit
Processors were scored with a figure of merit provided by the course staff, which weights execution time much more heavily than area:
\[
\text{Score} = \frac{10^{30}}{(\text{cycles} \times t_{clk})^3 \times \text{Area}}
\]
where cycles is the CoreMark cycle count, \(t_{clk}\) is the critical path length in ns, and Area is the total cell area in µm². Our priorities followed the weighting: first clock period through pipelining, then cycle count through branch prediction, then area through architectural cleanup.

title: Pipelined RISC-V Processor
text:
Processor Optimizations

Pipelining
The five stages are Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, and Writeback. Splitting each instruction across stages shortens the critical path and lets several instructions execute concurrently. Our first pipelined version cut the single-cycle processor’s 8.24 ns critical path to 5.10 ns. We considered a sixth stage, but the 3 ns instruction and data memories put a floor on the clock period, so the extra stage would not have paid off.


Multiply Unit






Figure 2: The 3-stage multiply unit.



The multiply unit (Figure 2) is a modified version of the Wally multiplier. In the first stage, it computes the four pieces of partial product PP1 with four 16×16 multiplications, along with the sign-correction partial products PP2 through PP4. In the second stage, the four pieces are summed into PP1, all four partial products are added into a 64-bit result, and the upper or lower half is selected based on the instruction.
The M1 register keeps the partial product calculation off the critical path. This adds two cycles to every multiply, but the shorter critical path more than makes up for it. When a multiply enters Execute, a counter waits two cycles and then resets. While the unit is busy, the rest of the pipeline stalls, which keeps the existing hazard logic correct.
// Four 16x16 multiplies — true HALF x HALF critical path
assign PP1E_ll = Aprime_lo * Bprime_lo;
assign PP1E_lh = Aprime_lo * Bprime_hi;
assign PP1E_hl = Aprime_hi * Bprime_lo;
assign PP1E_hh = Aprime_hi * Bprime_hi;


Branch Logic






Figure 3: Branch resolution logic in the Execute stage.



The branch logic decides whether the next PC is PC+4 or the branch target. Instead of a 6-way multiplexer that evaluates each branch type separately, it takes advantage of how RISC-V encodes funct3: bits [2:1] select the comparison and bit [0] selects its polarity.



Funct3[2:1]
Base Flag
Instructions




00
FlagsE[0] (Zero)
BEQ, BNE


10
FlagsE[1] (Less Than)
BLT, BGE


11
FlagsE[2] (Less Than Unsigned)
BLTU, BGEU



An XOR gate then acts as a conditional inverter. When Funct3E[0] is 0 (e.g., BEQ) the output is the base flag; when it is 1 (e.g., BNE) the output is the inverted flag. This cut the logic from about 60 transistors for a 6-way mux to about 36 for a 3-way mux plus XOR.
always_comb begin
    case (Funct3E[2:1])
        2'b00: base_flag = FlagsE[0]; // BEQ / BNE
        2'b10: base_flag = FlagsE[1]; // BLT / BGE
        2'b11: base_flag = FlagsE[2]; // BLTU / BGEU
        default: base_flag = 1'b0;
    endcase
end

assign BranchTaken = base_flag ^ Funct3E[0];


Optimized Synthesis
The processor was synthesized with Synopsys Design Compiler on SkyWater SKY130, an open-source 130 nm PDK. Since the memories have a 3 ns access time, the critical path cannot be shorter than 3 ns, so we targeted 333 MHz to land exactly on that limit. With timing effectively capped, we also told the tool to minimize area.
We enabled the maxopt flag, which runs the following:
if { $maxopt == 1 } {
    ungroup -all -simple_names -flatten
    compile_ultra -retime
    optimize_registers
}

ungroup -all -simple_names -flatten removes the module hierarchy and flattens the design into a single netlist, so the compiler can optimize across module boundaries.
compile_ultra -retime runs the full set of optimizations (datapath optimization, constant propagation, logic restructuring) and lets the compiler move registers across combinational logic to balance path delays.
optimize_registers is a second pass focused on register placement: moving registers to reduce setup time, merging redundant ones, and rebalancing pipeline registers across the flattened netlist.

The final synthesis settings were:
SYNTH_MAKE_FLAGS ?= \
    OUTPUTBASEDIR=$(WORK_DIR) \
    NAME=lynn \
    DESIGN=$(SYNTH_TOP) \
    SYNTH_FILES=$(SYNTH_FILES) \
    LIB_FILES=$(LIB_FILES) \
    PROCESSORTOP=$(PROCESSOR_TOP) \
    INCDIR=$(INC_DIR) \
    CONFIG=- \
    MOD=- \
    HDLDIR=$(PROCESSOR_DIR) \
    LYNN=1 \
    TECH=$(SYNTH_TECH) \
    MAXOPT=1 \
    FREQ=333 \
    MAXCORES=4


Minimizing Area
To reduce area we focused on removing registers. A single unoptimized 32-bit register synthesizes to about 1,300 µm², roughly 0.7% of the final processor, so each one removed made a noticeable difference in score.
Trimming the CSR file. Our first CSR file kept counters for every instruction class (R-type, jumps, branches, loads, etc.). We removed everything except instructions retired and clock cycles, which shrank the CSR file by about 50,000 µm².
Merging pipelined signals. We had been carrying PC+4 and PCTarget all the way to Writeback. Instead, we route them into ALUResult in Execute and let the writeback mux select ALUResult. This removed four 32-bit pipeline registers and shrank the writeback mux. Similarly, CSRReadData and ImmExtD are muxed together in Decode (selected by CSRSrcD) into a single SharedDataE register, which removed another 32-bit register.
Simplifying the hazard unit. Removing the RdE != 0 check from the load-use stall logic (so the processor stalls even when a load writes x0) raised the score by about 1%.






Figure 4: Per-module area breakdown of the final processor.



As Figure 4 shows, the register file and multiply unit together make up about two-thirds of the processor’s area.


Hazard Unit






Figure 5: Hazard unit logic.



The hazard unit (Figure 5) resolves data hazards by forwarding from Memory or Writeback, and stalls for load-use hazards, inserting a bubble into Execute. It flushes Decode when a branch is predicted taken, and flushes both Decode and Execute on a misprediction. We tuned it to stall or flush only when strictly necessary, reducing the total cycle count. While a multiply is in progress, the hazard unit stalls every stage.
logic lwStall;
assign lwStall = ResultSrcE0 & ((Rs1D == RdE) | (Rs2D == RdE));

assign StallF  = lwStall | MulBusy;
assign StallD  = lwStall | MulBusy;

// Flush Decode if we mispredict in execute OR if we predict taken in decode
assign FlushD  = MispredictE | PredictTakenD;
// Flush Execute if there's a load stall OR if we mispredict in execute
assign FlushE  = lwStall | MispredictE;


Branch Prediction
After the second checkpoint, we added a branch target buffer (BTB) and a 2-bit branch predictor in the Fetch stage to reduce the cycle count.






Figure 6: Branch target buffer in the Fetch stage (not used in the final design).



The BTB derives a 3-bit index from PCF[4:2] and a 10-bit tag from PCF[14:5]. If the tag matches a valid entry in btb_ram, it asserts BTBHitF, and the PC logic selects the predicted target. That target is computed by shifting the stored offset left by two, sign-extending it to 32 bits, and adding it to PCF. We swept the BTB size across several synthesis runs:



Index Bits
CoreMark/MHz
Figure of Merit




2 (4 slots)
2.88
3,749


3 (8 slots)
2.95
4,085.3


4 (16 slots)
3.00
4,000


5 (32 slots)
3.03
3,227



The BTB raised CoreMark/MHz, but it cost area and timing. With the BTB and 2-bit predictor, the processor grew to 214,931 µm² (the BTB alone was 6.7% of it) and the critical path lengthened to 3.17 ns.






Figure 7: Critical path with the BTB, highlighted in pink.



As Figure 7 shows, the critical path now ran through the combinational logic that generates FlushE, since it depends on both PredictTakenE and PCSrcE.
Based on this, we designed a predictor with minimal area overhead and no impact on the critical path that still improved CoreMark: always predict backward branches taken.






Figure 8: Backward-taken static branch predictor used in the final design.



A negative branch offset (ImmExtD[31] = 1) usually indicates a loop, so the predictor (Figure 8) predicts taken whenever a branch has a negative offset, and always predicts JAL taken. PCNext is then set to the predicted target. A correctly predicted taken branch costs one cycle; a misprediction costs two. This raised CoreMark/MHz from 2.83 to 2.91 and is the predictor used in the final processor.
// Predict branches taken if offset is negative (ImmExtD[31]).
// Predict JAL (JumpD & ~JalrD) as always taken.
assign PredictedTargetD = PCD + ImmExtD;
assign PredictTakenD = (BranchD & ImmExtD[31]) | (JumpD & ~JalrD);

title: Pipelined RISC-V Processor
text:
Verification
We verified the processor with two suites. The ACT4 architectural compliance tests check that each instruction produces the correct result, and CoreMark shows how the processor handles a real program. We found that ACT4 alone was not thorough enough to catch the pipelining bugs that later showed up in CoreMark.

ACT4
The final processor passes all 45 ACT4 tests for RV32I, Zicntr, Zihpm, and Zmmul:
=== Test Log Summary ===
Total logs:                 45
Passed:                     45
Failed:                     0
Missing 'Completed':        0
Unreadable:                 0


CoreMark
CoreMark runs with zero errors on the final processor, with a CoreMark/MHz score of 2.91 and a CPI of 1.19:
WALLY CoreMark Results (from get_time)
  Elapsed MTIME: 3425167
  Elapsed MINSTRET: 2864107
  COREMARK/MHz Score: 10,000,000 / 3425167 = 2.91
  CPI: 3425167 / 2864107 = 1.19
2K performance run parameters for coremark.
CoreMark Size    : 666
Total ticks      : 3425167
Iterations       : 10
Compiler version : GCC15.2.0
INFO: Test Completed!


A Bug ACT4 Missed






Figure 9: Earlier version of the multiply unit that failed CoreMark.



At one point the processor passed every ACT4 test but produced wrong results in CoreMark:
[0]ERROR! list crc 0xec70 - should be 0xe714
[0]ERROR! matrix crc 0xb9d6 - should be 0x1fd7
[0]ERROR! state crc 0xb215 - should be 0x8e3a
The cause was stall logic in an earlier version of the multiply unit (Figure 9) that failed to stall the second of two back-to-back multiplies. This corner case only exists in a pipelined processor. ACT4 checks that each multiply instruction gives the right answer on its own, but never issues two in a row. It was a hard bug to track down, and a rewarding one to fix.

Pipelining (Checkpoint 1) and the faster multiplier with optimized synthesis (Checkpoint 2) produced most of the improvement. Branch prediction and area reduction added the final 14%. Pipelining lowers CoreMark/MHz, since stalls and flushes push CPI above 1, but the much shorter clock period more than compensates.
We had projected a figure of merit of 7,190, and the final score of 4,814 fell short. We beat our predicted clock period of 3.86 ns, and our final area came in at about half of our estimate. However, we did not implement any new extensions that would have reduced the cycle count. We also expected to gain by compiling CoreMark more aggressively, but the provided build was already fully optimized.

title: Pipelined RISC-V Processor
text:
Physical Layout
The class flow stops at synthesis, so after the project I took the final RTL through a full place-and-route to see what the processor would look like as a chip. I used the open-source OpenROAD flow on the same SkyWater SKY130 process: Yosys synthesized the design to 10,580 standard cells, and OpenROAD floorplanned, placed, built the clock tree, and routed every wire. The routed layout was then merged with the real transistor-level layouts of the SKY130 standard cells, so the images below come directly from the chip’s mask geometry. The 3D model at the top of this page is built from the same data: the die’s surface textures are baked from the mask layers, and the close-up extrudes every polygon in an 18 × 16 µm patch to SKY130’s actual layer heights.






Figure 10: The full 526 × 526 µm die. The gold horizontal and silver vertical stripes are the top two metal layers, which carry power across the chip. The empty patch in the upper left holds only filler cells, since the logic only needs about 55% of the core.



Zooming in shows the layers underneath. In Figure 11, the signal wiring on metal layers 1 through 3 runs on a fixed grid of tracks beneath the power stripes.






Figure 11: An 80 × 60 µm region with the power grid and signal routing.



With the upper metal layers removed (Figure 12), the rows of standard cells appear. The copper bands are the power and ground rails that every cell in a row shares, and the green vertical wires are metal 2 connecting cells across rows.






Figure 12: A 24 × 16 µm region with metal 3 and above removed.



At the smallest scale (Figure 13), the individual transistors are visible. Each orange polysilicon line that crosses a green diffusion region is a transistor gate, the gray local interconnect wires transistors together into gates and flip-flops, and the metal 1 wires above connect those cells to each other.






Figure 13: A 12 × 7 µm region down to metal 1. Each orange line crossing green diffusion is a single transistor.



This layout is an illustration rather than a signoff-quality chip. I capped the detailed router early, so it still has unresolved spacing violations. Yosys also builds the multiplier from ripple-carry adders instead of the fast DesignWare components Design Compiler uses, so this netlist is much slower than our 3.02 ns result, and the tools aren’t sizing cells against the same timing target. The timing and area numbers in this report come from Design Compiler.

title: Pipelined RISC-V Processor
text:
Future Improvements






Figure 14: Planned 6-stage pipeline with the Execute stage split in two (not implemented).



Our next step would be to split the Execute stage in two (Figure 14). The ALU source-select muxes would sit in the first half, since their inputs arrive from across the processor, which would shorten the critical path and let the multiplier pipeline without stalling.
That second change matters. In an earlier lab, we found that CoreMark executes 173,933 multiplies. Because the processor currently stalls on every multiply, each one adds stall cycles. That costs about 5% of performance compared to the 3,248,907 total cycles we measured without the multi-cycle multiplier.

title: Pipelined RISC-V Processor
text:
Reflection

Teamwork
Max and I were both genuinely interested in this project, which kept us motivated. We communicated frequently, held design reviews to agree on architectural decisions, worked through implementation details together, and kept a detailed log of progress and goals.
For future projects, we would change two things. First, we would invest more in high-level planning before starting implementation, so we weren’t building without a clear plan and could make better architectural decisions up front. Second, we would use our time together more efficiently. Near the end of the project, much of our shared time went to waiting on synthesis runs.


Use of AI
AI was most useful for debugging and for suggesting synthesis improvements. When wiring units together it is easy to mix up signals, and AI was good at spotting those bugs and checking combinational Verilog before compilation. It was not always right: Copilot’s autocomplete sometimes invented signal names while we were connecting modules, and it led us astray while debugging the hazard unit.
We learned to debug on our own first before asking for help, which gave us a better sense of the possible causes. We also found that giving the model a diagram of the processor helped it understand our code and suggest better fixes.

title: Pierce Clark
text: I’m an engineering student at Harvey Mudd College. I like working where hardware and software meet: designing digital logic, figuring out how processors work, and writing the low-level code that brings a board to life.

title: Pierce Clark
text:
What I Study

Computer Architecture
How processors are built and what makes them fast. For my System-on-Chip Design final project, my partner and I turned a single-cycle RISC-V core into a 5-stage pipelined processor and optimized it for speed and area. I’ve also worked on RISC-V’s debug trigger extension, which adds hardware breakpoints and watchpoints to the architecture.


Design & Verification
Writing SystemVerilog and proving it works with simulation, compliance tests, and benchmarks. As a Clay-Wolkin Research Fellow, I write certification tests for RISC-V Sdtrig, and I’ve found and reported bugs in a RISC-V reference simulator along the way.


Embedded Systems
Register-level microcontroller programming and real peripherals. In Microprocessor-based Systems (E155), I’ve used an iCE40 FPGA and an STM32L432KC to build a keypad scanner, digital audio, and a Wi-Fi temperature monitor over SPI.


Industry Hardware
At TRL11, I worked on space-qualified networking hardware.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
In lab 6, the STM32L432KC microcontroller was configured to use its built-in serial peripheral interface to communicate with a DS1722 Digital Thermometer. The microcontroller also communicated with an ESP8266 32-bit Wi-Fi micro-controller chip over UART. The ESP8266 displayed html code that allowed users to change the state of an LED on the board, and change the resolution of the temperature measurement.
This lab developed skills regarding configuring serial protocols. It also built on the skill of writing register-level drivers for microcontrollers.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
In lab 6, the STM32L432KC microcontroller was configured to use its built-in serial peripheral interface to communicate with a DS1722 Digital Thermometer. The microcontroller also communicated with an ESP8266 32-bit Wi-Fi micro-controller chip over UART. The ESP8266 displayed html code that allowed users to change the state of an LED on the board, and change the resolution of the temperature measurement.
This lab developed skills regarding configuring serial protocols. It also built on the skill of writing register-level drivers for microcontrollers.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Design
The SPI1 peripheral was configured to communicate with the DS1722 in full-duplex mode. This configuration uses four wires (CE, MISO, MOSI, SCLK).
The system clock on the microcontroller was set to PLL of 80 MHz. SPI1 is clocked from the APB2 bus, which was left at its default prescaler of 1, so \(f_{PCLK2} = 80\) MHz. The SPI clock is divided down from this by the baud rate control bits (BR) in SPI1_CR1:
\[
f_{SCLK} = \frac{f_{PCLK2}}{2^{BR+1}}
\]
With a baud rate setting of BR = 7 (0b111), the frequency of the SPI clock is
\[
f_{SCLK} = \frac{80\text{ MHz}}{2^{7+1}} = \frac{80\text{ MHz}}{256} = 312.5\text{ kHz}
\]
This is well below the DS1722’s maximum SCLK frequency of 5 MHz.
The PB3 pin was connected by GPIO to the LED. Pins PA9 and PA10 were used for the UART interface. I was provided pre-written drivers. The only important thing I had to do was to connect the MCU’s TX to the ESP8266’s RX, and vice versa.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Testing Methodology
Before flashing the MCU or connecting to the temperature or wifi sensors, the code was debugged in Segger Embedded Studio. I loaded the drivers and packages for my STM32L432KC MCU, and made sure the code was compiling and had no syntax errors. The SPI functionality was confirmed using an oscilloscope.

Oscilloscope
The ideal SPI protocol is described in the DS1722 datasheet, shown below.



SPI multiple byte burst transfer from the DS1722 datasheet (Figure 6).


To read from the temperature sensor, the address and data bytes are shifted MSB first into the serial data input (SDI) and out of the serial data output (SDO). As per the datasheet, any transfer requires the address of the byte to specify a write or a read, followed by one or more bytes of data. The temperature measurement is 2 bytes, meaning we will use a 3-byte burst to read 2 bytes from the address provided in the first byte. To read the temperature, we set the address to 0x01.



Oscilloscope capture of a 3-byte SPI read of the DS1722 temperature registers.


The SPI functionality was verified using an oscilloscope to measure all 4 wires. The waveforms confirm that the SPI setup is performing as expected. CE begins by going high. In the first byte, the MCU sends the address 0x01 on MOSI. In the second and third bytes, the MCU sends test data 0x56 and 0x73. The DS1722 shifts out the temperature on MISO, giving us the LSB (0x40), then MSB (0x14). This gives a reading of 0x1440, or 20.25 °C (68.45°F), which is a reasonable room temperature.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated GitHub repository.

Schematic



Schematic of the Lab 6 circuit, showing the MCU connected to the ESP8266 over UART, the DS1722 over SPI, and the LED on PB3.


The STM32L432KC connects to the DS1722 over SPI1 (SCLK on PA5, MISO on PA6, MOSI on PB5, CE on PB0), to the ESP8266 over UART (TX on PA9, RX on PA10), and drives the LED on PB3 through a 510 Ω resistor.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Results and Discussion
All requirements for the lab were met. The temperature sensor accurately displayed the temperature on the website. Input from the website was able to change the floating point resolution of the measurement.

Website



Webpage served by the ESP8266, with LED control buttons, temperature resolution buttons, and the current temperature reading.


The webpage served by the ESP8266 is shown above. Users can turn the LED on or off and select a temperature resolution from 8 to 12 bits. The page displays the current LED status, the selected resolution, and the temperature read from the DS1722.


Shortcomings
In terms of shortcomings, the reference manual for the SPI is difficult to understand. I would say I understand SPI to a high degree; however, I would likely benefit by creating a system that customizes the SPI configuration more, such as a multi-master or one-way communication system.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Conclusion
In conclusion, in lab 6, SPI was used to interface with a temperature sensor. UART was used to send website info to an ESP8266. This allows people connected to the ESP8266’s wifi network to monitor the temperature sensor’s output with varying amounts of resolution.
In total, I spent ~13 hours on this lab.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Lab 6 AI Prototype

Model
I used Claude Opus 5.5 at High effort


Frontend Prompt
I’m making a web portal to interface with a temperature sensor. Create a HTML page that looks good and is intuitive to show the temperature, control an LED, and change the precision of the readout.

Process
I used Claude Code to make a branch of my code and integrate the HTML into the existing codebase.


Results
The AI-generated webpage is shown in Figure 1. Compared to my webpage in the Website section, it displays the temperature in both °C and °F with a color scale, uses a toggle for the LED with an indicator light, and labels each precision setting with its step size. It also adds a connection indicator and an auto-refresh option that updates the reading every 5 seconds.






Figure 1: AI-generated webpage, showing the temperature at 12-bit precision, the LED toggle, and the precision selector.






Embedded Prompt
Write me a C function to carry out a SPI transaction to retrieve a temperature reading from a DS1722 sensor. Use CMSIS libraries for the STM32L432KC.

Process
The code looks like it works, I loaded the AI prototype branch with the drivers integrated, and the website ran just like before. This indicates the drivers are functioning correctly.


Results
uint8_t ds1722ReadReg(uint8_t addr) {
    ceHigh();
    shortDelay();
    spiXfer(addr & 0x7F);              // address byte, A7 = 0 for read
    uint8_t val = spiXfer(0x00);       // dummy byte clocks the data out
    while (SPI1->SR & SPI_SR_BSY);     // let the last clock finish before dropping CE
    ceLow();
    shortDelay();
    return val;
}



Comparison
The LLM generated frontend web code better than low-level embedded C. I would say that for C, it might overcomplicate the drivers trying to make them more safe. For the application, I think my driver was more readable than the AI’s.


Reflection
I would rate the output quality very high. The generated code, although it functions identically, provides a much better UI, and a clean device driver. The LLM’s explanation of the driver was quite limited, but it left a fair amount of documentation in the driver that helps a lot.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, a design was implemented on the Lattice iCE40 UP5K to practice basic FPGA programming. The on-board 48 MHz high-speed oscillator was divided down with a counter to blink an on-board LED at ~2.4 Hz. Four on-board switches drove a seven segment display and two additional on-board LEDs.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The on-board high-speed oscillator, HSOSC, from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library generated a 48 MHz clock. A counter divided that clock to drive one on-board LED, and combinational logic on the switch bits drove the other two.
The seven segment display module took 4 on-board switches as input and used case logic to select the segment pattern for the matching hexadecimal character.
Testbenches were written for every module, sweeping all inputs where that was feasible.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository.

Block Diagram


Show block diagram




Figure 1: Block diagram of the Verilog design.



The block diagram in Figure 1 shows the overall architecture of the design. The top level module includes 3 submodules which contain the HSOSC, counter divider, and display logic.


Schematic


Show schematic




Figure 2: Schematic of the physical circuit.



Figure 2 shows the physical layout. The display is powered from the 3.3 V pin, and the FPGA pins ground each segment to light it. 1 kΩ series resistors limit the on-board LED currents, and 150 Ω resistors limit the seven-segment current, keeping both within the FPGA I/O and display ratings.


Clock Divider Calculations
The HSOSC module runs at its default rate of \(f_{clk} = 48\text{ MHz}\). A counter counts to \(N = 20{,}000{,}000\) and resets, and the LED is on whenever the count is greater than \(\frac12 N\), so one full on/off cycle takes \(N\) clock cycles:
\[
f_{blink} = \frac{f_{clk}}{N} = \frac{48 \times 10^6\text{ Hz}}{20 \times 10^6} = 2.4\text{ Hz}
\]
That matches the rate specified in the lab guide and the rate observed on the board.


Seven Segment Circuit Calculations



Figure 3: Seven segment display circuit.





Figure 4: Forward current versus forward voltage for the seven segment display, taken from the HDSP-511A datasheet.


Each segment of the display is an LED with an absolute maximum current rating of 30 mA. The circuit was designed for a target current of \(I = 8\text{ mA}\).
Each segment of the display is driven from the 3.3 V pin, \(V_{cc} = 3.3\text{ V}\), and has a diode forward voltage of \(V_f = 1.8\text{ V}\) at the target current, as shown in Figure 4. The remaining voltage is dropped across the current-limiting series resistor:
\[
V_R = V_{cc} - V_f = 3.3\text{ V} - 1.8\text{ V} = 1.5\text{ V}
\]
Applying Ohm’s law across the resistor gives the required resistance:
\[
R = \frac{V_R}{I} = \frac{1.5\text{ V}}{8\text{ mA}} = 187.5\,\Omega
\]
A standard \(150\,\Omega\) resistor was used in the final design. It draws \(1.5\text{ V} / 150\,\Omega = 10\text{ mA}\) per segment, which is slightly above the 8 mA target but still well under the 30 mA maximum rating.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Results and Discussion

Testbench Simulation


Show testbench simulation




Figure 5: A QuestaSim simulation of the top level module, showing the switch inputs, the seven segment outputs, the internal oscillator, and the counter driving the LED.



Figure 5 shows the QuestaSim results for the top level testbench. Each switch input produced the expected seven segment pattern, and the LED output followed the counter, staying high for the top half of each cycle. The counter in the testbench was given a cycle length of ten clock cycles to demonstrate the reset functionality.

text:
Conclusion
The design implemented all three LED behaviors. The on-board high-speed oscillator blinked the on-board LED, and the seven segment display showed all 16 outputs correctly. This lab took at least 20 hours.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
In lab 4, the STM32L432KC microcontroller was programmed to play music through an 8-ohm speaker. The speaker was driven by a LM386 audio amplifier. Musical notes were store as a list of pitches (Hz) and durations (ms), which the microcontroller interpreted to program timer peripherals in order to create a wave of the same pitch.
This lab developed skills such as reading datasheets and creating register-level drivers for microcontrollers.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
In lab 4, the STM32L432KC microcontroller was programmed to play music through an 8-ohm speaker. The speaker was driven by a LM386 audio amplifier. Musical notes were store as a list of pitches (Hz) and durations (ms), which the microcontroller interpreted to program timer peripherals in order to create a wave of the same pitch.
This lab developed skills such as reading datasheets and creating register-level drivers for microcontrollers.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
The TIM16 timer peripheral was configured to create a PWM and overflows were counted to keep track of the notes duration.
System clock was set to MSI. In the APB2 bus, the prescaler was set to 3, which gave a input frequency of 1MHz to the timer.
The timer was set to PWM mode 1, which sets Channel 1 to active as long as \(TIM16_{CNT}<TIM16_{CCR1}\), else it is inactive.
The microcontroller read the overflow flag to keep track of the amount of clock overflows, then changes to the next note after a amount of overflows calculated from the notes duration.
The GPIO pin 6 was connected to TIM16 by writing registers MODER and AFRL. GPIO pin 6 (PA6) was externally connected to the LM386 audio amplifier. I used GPIO bank A on this design since it had the most external pins on the development board.
Defines were used to encode important addresses from the datasheet like the start of the GPIOA bank addresses. Structs were written to organize the register from the reference manual.
The design was tested using oscilloscopes to measure the frequency of the output by playing the Für Elise score.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository.

Schematic






Figure 1: Schematic of the physical circuit, showing the MCU GPIO output driving the LM386 amplifier and the 8 Ω speaker.



Circuit schematic used was from Texas Instruments LM386 Low Voltage Audio Power Amplifier datasheet


Frequency and Duration Calculations
Timer clock and prescaler calculations
\[
f_{timer} = \frac{f_{clk}}{PSC + 1} = \frac{4 \text{Mhz}}{3 + 1} = 1\text{Mhz}
\]
Auto-reload value for a note of frequency \(f_{note}\)
\[
ARR = \frac{f_{timer}}{f_{note}} - 1
\]
The final output frequency of the timers signal is:
\[
f_{out} = \frac{f_{timer}}{ARR + 1}
\]
A note lasting \(t\) milliseconds last for \(n\) overflows, and the actual duration played is
\[
n = \frac{f_{note} * t}{1000}
\]
\[
t_{out} = \frac{n * (ARR + 1)}{f_{timer}}
\]

Example Calculations
Both examples use a 250 ms note.
Example 1: 220 Hz
\[
ARR = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{220\text{ Hz}} - 1 = 4545 - 1 = 4544
\]
\[
f_{out} = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{4544 + 1} = 220.02\text{ Hz}
\]
\[
n = \frac{220\text{ Hz} * 250\text{ ms}}{1000} = 55
\]
\[
t_{out} = \frac{55 * 4545}{1000000\text{ Hz}} = 0.249975\text{ s} = 249.975\text{ ms}
\]
Example 2: 1000 Hz
\[
ARR = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{1000\text{ Hz}} - 1 = 999
\]
\[
f_{out} = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{999 + 1} = 1000\text{ Hz}
\]
\[
n = \frac{1000\text{ Hz} * 250\text{ ms}}{1000} = 250
\]
\[
t_{out} = \frac{250 * 1000}{1000000\text{ Hz}} = 0.25\text{ s} = 250\text{ ms}
\]
Both example notes show that the system can create 220 Hz and 1000 Hz pitches within 1% accuracy.


Absolute Max/Min Frequency and Duration
Minimum frequency
TIM16 is a 16 bit timer, so the largest ARR is 65535. The lowest frequency is
\[
f_{min} = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{65535 + 1} = 15.26\text{ Hz}
\]
Maximum frequency
The fastest we can make the timer output is with a cycle 2 ticks long, since we need one half to be on for the PWM signal to output.
\[
ARR + 1 = 2
\]
\[
f_{max} = \frac{1000000\text{ Hz}}{1 + 1} = 500000\text{ Hz} = 500\text{ kHz}
\]
Minimum duration
The minimum duration for a note is \(N = 1\) overflows
\[
t_{min} = \frac{1000}{f_{note}}\text{ ms}
\]
At the highest frequency, 500 kHz:
\[
t_{min} = \frac{1000}{500000}\text{ ms} = 0.002\text{ ms} = 2\text{ µs}
\]
Practically however, the minimum is 1 ms because durations are stored as integer milliseconds.
Maximum duration
\(n\) is computed with uint32_t, so \(f_{note} * t\) must stay below 4294967295. The longest note is possible at the lowest frequency, 16 Hz:
\[
t_{max} = \frac{4294967295}{16}\text{ ms} = 268435455\text{ ms} = 74.6\text{ hours}
\]
The timer is able to play fur elise all within 1% accuracy, since nearly all the notes fall close withing the range of 200-1000 Hz. This was additionally proven by calculating the error for every note in the song in a spreadsheet.(https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Ons0ZR9uOKoXykoLUrtP-t-9wVeZpt0yylUZN51Lkxk/edit?usp=sharing)

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Results and Discussion
All requirements for the lab were met. The songs were successfully played through the speaker circuit.

Shortcomings
In terms of shortcomings, the reference manual was intitially overwhelming, so much control+f was used to find features of interest.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Conclusion
In conclusion, in Lab 4, a STM32L432KC was used to drive a 8 ohm speaker. The code was able to play notes accurately within 1% of the desired pitch and duration. The song “The Hall of the Mountain King” was also play, although it was translated into notes by AI because I am not a music major.
In total, I spent ~15 hours on this lab.

Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text: In lab 3, a keypad scanner feeding a time multiplexed dual seven segment display on the iCE40 UP5K fpga. When a new key is pressed on the keypad, the new key press shifts into the right digit, old digit shifts left. This lab helped build skills involing FSM design, synchronizing and debouncing inputs.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text: In lab 3, a keypad scanner feeding a time multiplexed dual seven segment display on the iCE40 UP5K fpga. When a new key is pressed on the keypad, the new key press shifts into the right digit, old digit shifts left. This lab helped build skills involing FSM design, synchronizing and debouncing inputs.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
Input synchronizers were used on all outside inputs to the fpga (reset, keyboard columns). A debouncer fsm waits for a set amount of time based on a variable flip_bit to debounce the 4 column signals from the keyboard. A scanner toggles rows to check for key presses using a 48 MHz HSOSC divided by 480,000.
A keypad decoder tells us what key is being pressed, and a keypad reader fsm determines when to update the display based on the keypad. The two digits are display on a reused module from Lab 2, which is multiplexed at 100 hz. Currently, no solution has been made to capture multiple key presses simultaineously, although solutions such as an additional state in the keypad reader have been proposed.
Each module that was not used in lab 2 has a testbench that expresses all FSM states or input to combinational logic.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository.

Block Diagram






Figure 1: Block diagram of top-level design, showing the input synchronizers and debouncers, keypad decoder, keypad reader, scanner, and display logic.



In this diagram we can see the general layout of the circuit. Synchronizer modules are present on all inputs to the fpga. A debouncer is placed on the columns in order to prevent switch bouncing from the keyboard. The Keypad Decoder tell us what key is being pressed. While the Keypade Reader module choses when to update the display, and feeds the data to the display module.


Schematic






Figure 2: Schematic of the physical circuit, showing the matrix keypad with 1 kΩ column pull-ups and transistor row drivers, and the HDSP-5721 dual seven segment display with 100 Ω segment resistors and transistor digit drivers. Note: Vdd = 3.3V



In this schematic, we see the general circuit layout for the lab. The keyboard has pull-ups on the column inputs, and row drivers. The display transistors and resistors are also shown. The schematic for this lab is effectively the same as lab 2.


State transition diagram






Figure 3: State transition diagram of the keypad reader FSM, showing the SCAN, PRESS, and HOLD states.



States:
SCAN: Allows the scanner to scan the rows until it detects a column pressed.
PRESS: The current key is stored in d0, and the old d0 goes to d1.
HOLD: Remains held until the all keys in the row are released.


Calculations
The scanner goes to the next row once every 480,000 cycles of the 48 MHz HSOSC clock:
\[
f_{row} = \frac{48\text{ MHz}}{480{,}000} = 100\text{ Hz}
\] \[
T_{row} = \frac{1}{100\text{ Hz}} = 10\text{ ms}
\]
Each row is driven for 10 ms before the scanner moves on. A 40 ms sweep is short compared to a typical human key press, so every press is seen on at least one full sweep.
The debounce time waits for \(2^{17}\) cycles at 48 MHz, which equates to a wait time of 2.7 ms. Switch bounces do not last this long on average.
The display resistors values and transistor configuration are identical the Lab 2. See Lab 2 writeup for reference.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text:
Results and Discussion
All profiency requirements were met on the board, however it lacks a way to detect more than one keypress at a time.

Testbench Simulation


Show top-level waveforms







Figure 4: QuestaSim simulation of the top-level module.

Figure 6: QuestaSim simulation of the debouncer.

Each module was tested with a testbench. FSM’s were cycled through all states, and reset. Combinational logic in the decoder was stressed using all possible input.

The final design successfully detected all keypad presses without double presses from bouncing. In total, I spent 13-15 hours on this lab.

text:
Lab 3 AI Prototype

Model
The model used was Opus 5.5, the newest and most powerful frontier model at this time.


Prompt
Target device: Lattice iCE40 UP5K FPGA with internal high-speed oscillator (~20 MHz).

Write synthesizable SystemVerilog to scan a 4x4 matrix keypad and display the last two hex keys pressed on a dual 7‑segment display. Implement:

A clock divider that derives a scan clock on the order of 100–200 Hz from the internal oscillator.
A keypad scanning controller that iterates one active‑low column at a time and samples active‑low rows, registering at most one key per press (debounce‑by‑design), ignoring additional presses while any key is held, and allowing a new registration only after release.
A top level that updates two hex digits (older and most recent) when a new key is registered and drives a time‑multiplexed two‑digit 7‑segment display without visible flicker and with balanced brightness.
Use idiomatic SystemVerilog (e.g., logic, always_ff, enumerated states for FSMs). Provide clean module boundaries and keep all state synchronous. Include brief comments explaining the design choices.


Process






Figure 9: Summary of the steps Claude took while generating the AI prototype.



Claude took some interesting steps during its response. Most interestingly, it download verilator in order to simulate and debug its own code before giving it to me. This already gives me extreme confidence that this code will compile and run when I put it in Questa.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display and Keypad Scanner
text: In this lab, a design was implemented on the Lattice iCE40 UP5K to practice designing sequential circuits and use transistors. Two independent hexadecimal digits were displayed on a dual seven segment display using a single decoder module and time multiplexing. A scanning module driven at 8 Hz swept the keypad rows and read the columns, lighting on-board LEDs to indicate which keys were pressed.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display and Keypad Scanner
text: In this lab, a design was implemented on the Lattice iCE40 UP5K to practice designing sequential circuits and use transistors. Two independent hexadecimal digits were displayed on a dual seven segment display using a single decoder module and time multiplexing. A scanning module driven at 8 Hz swept the keypad rows and read the columns, lighting on-board LEDs to indicate which keys were pressed.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display and Keypad Scanner
text:
Design and Testing Methodology

Time Multiplexed Display
The on-board high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library was used to generate a clock signal at 48 MHz. A counter was used to divide the high frequency clock signal down to 100hz. That blinking frequency was used to toggle the power between the seven segment displays. The design was tested using an automatic test bench to demonstrate that the correct signal was passed when the display was flipped between digits.


Keypad Scanner
The on-board high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library was used to generate a clock signal at 48 MHz. counter was used to divide the high frequency clock signal down to 8hz, and toggle a 4-state FSM such that each state was entered twice a second (2hz). The keypads output was read using inputs and then inverted due the active low behavior of the keypad.


Testing
Testbenches were written for the scanner and top level module to demonstrate that the state transitions happened correctly. The oscilliscope was also used to verify the circuitry performed as expected.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed Seven Segment Display and Keypad Scanner
text:
Technical Documentation
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository.

Block Diagram


Show block diagram




Figure 1: Top level block diagram of the Verilog design.



The block diagram in Figure 1 shows the overall architecture of the design. The top level module includes 3 submodules which contain the HSOSC, counter with muxing logic, scanner module, and display logic.


Schematic


Show seven segment display schematic




Figure 2: Schematic of the multiplexed seven segment display circuit. All FPGA pins in this circuit are configured in 100 kΩ pull-up mode.



Figure 2 shows the physical layout. The display is powered from 2 PNP transistors from the 3.3 V pin. The FPGA pins toggle between these power pins, and ground each segment to light it. 100 Ω resistors limit the seven-segment current, keeping both within the FPGA I/O and display ratings.


Show keypad scanner schematic




Figure 3: Schematic of the keypad scanner circuit.



Figure 2 shows the physical layout. The display is powered from the 3.3 V pin, and the FPGA pins ground each segment to light it. 1 kΩ series resistors limit the on-board LED currents, and 150 Ω resistors limit the seven-segment current, keeping both within the FPGA I/O and display ratings.


Display Current and Segment Resistor Calculations
The display is an HDSP-5721, a two digit common anode seven segment display. Its datasheet has a typical forward voltage of \(V_F = 2.0\text{ V}\) per segment at 20 mA.
Each segment is in series between the anode and an FPGA pin, with a \(100\,\Omega\) series resistor. The segments are driven from 3.3 V through a 2N3906 PNP transistor. The equation for the circuit is \(V_{cc} = V_{EC(sat)} + V_F + I_F R\). Taking \(V_{BE(sat)} = 0.25\text{ V}\) for the 2N3906, \(V_F = 2.0\text{ V}\) leaves 1.05 V across the resistor:
\[
I_F = \frac{V_{cc} - V_{BE(sat)} - V_F}{R}
    = \frac{3.3 - 0.25 - 2.0}{100\,\Omega}
    = \frac{1.05\text{ V}}{100\,\Omega} = 10.5\text{ mA}
\]
Because the two digits are time multiplexed, each segment is lit for half of each multiplexing period, so the average current per segment is \(I_{avg} = I_F / 2 = 5.25\text{ mA}\). This is under the max current rating of the anode.


PNP Anode Driver Calculations
Each common anode is switched by a 2N3906 PNP. The emitter is 3.3 V, the collector drives one digit. The base is driven by a \(330\,\Omega\) resistor from an FPGA pin.
If all seven segments are lit at once, the total current drawn is 73.5 mA, which is less than the maximum 200mA Continuous Collector Current.
\[
I_C = 7 \times 10.5\text{ mA} = 73.5\text{ mA}
\]
With an emitter-base saturation voltage of \(V_{EB(sat)} = 0.8\text{ V}\), the base current is
\[
I_B = \frac{V_{cc} - V_{BE(sat)}}{R_B}
    = \frac{2.5\text{ V}}{330\,\Omega} = 7.6\text{ mA}
\]


NPN Open Drain Keypad Driver Calculations
Each row is driven through a 2N3904 NPN. The emitter is grounded, the collector drives the row, and the base is driven through a \(470\,\Omega\) resistor from an FPGA pin.
With \(V_{OH} = 3.3\text{ V}\) and \(V_{BE(sat)} = 0.8\text{ V}\), the base current is
\[
I_B = \frac{V_{OH} - V_{BE(sat)}}{R_B}
    = \frac{2.5\text{ V}}{470\,\Omega} = 5.3\text{ mA}
\]

Writing Certification Tests for RISC-V Sdtrig
text: Over the past several months, I’ve been working as a Clay-Wolkin Research Fellow on the RISC-V Architectural Certification Tests (ACTs). The ACTs are a set of assembly-language tests that certify whether a processor faithfully implements the RISC-V specification. My focus has been Sdtrig, the debug trigger extension. This post covers what Sdtrig is, how a certification test goes from a sentence in the spec to an executable test, and a few things I’ve learned along the way.

title: Writing Certification Tests for RISC-V Sdtrig
text:
What Sdtrig Is
Sdtrig defines a trigger module: a set of hardware triggers that watch the processor and take an action when a condition is met. Software selects a trigger with the tselect CSR and configures it through tdata1, tdata2, and tdata3. A trigger can watch for:

an instruction executing at a particular address,
a load or store to a particular address, or of a particular data value,
a number of instructions retiring (icount), or
an interrupt or exception.

When a trigger fires, it can raise a breakpoint exception or put the hart into Debug Mode. This is how hardware breakpoints and watchpoints in a debugger like GDB work.
Sdtrig is hard to test because so much of it is optional. Most trigger fields are WARL (write any, read legal), so an implementation can choose which trigger types, match modes, and sizes it supports. A certification test has to exercise everything an implementation claims to support, while accepting any legal choice it makes.

title: Writing Certification Tests for RISC-V Sdtrig
text:
From Spec to Test
My work has followed the pipeline the ACTs use for every extension.
1. Normative rules. Before you can test a spec, you have to identify each requirement in it. I tagged the normative rules in the Sdtrig chapters of the RISC-V Debug Specification. I then wrote the normative rule mapping that links each rule to the test plan, so every requirement is traceable to the test that checks it. My first contribution to the project was a smaller version of the same thing, a rule mapping for ExceptionsF.
2. Configuration parameters. Since so much of Sdtrig is implementation-defined, the tests need to know what a given processor supports. I added Sdtrig parameters to the RISC-V Unified Database (UDB). They describe which trigger types each trigger supports and which values each WARL field accepts. The test generators read these parameters to decide which tests to emit.
3. Coverpoints and test generators. A coverpoint describes one behavior that must be exercised, and a test generator produces the assembly that exercises it. My largest PR (about 5,000 lines across 28 files) added the Sdtrig test generators for machine, supervisor, and user mode. Since the Sail reference model doesn’t support Sdtrig, it also added a Whisper configuration that uses Spike as the reference instead.
Since then I’ve been extending coverage and keeping the pieces consistent. I unified the mcontrol6 coverpoints, generator, and test plan so they all describe the same set of tests. I’ve also opened PRs for trigger tests on atomic instructions and instruction counting and on cache-management operations, and split each section of the plan into its own generator.

title: Writing Certification Tests for RISC-V Sdtrig
text:
Bugs Found Along the Way
Certification tests are only useful if they catch real disagreements with the spec, and the Sdtrig tests turned up two in Whisper, Tenstorrent’s RISC-V reference simulator:

Wrong mtval on a trigger breakpoint. A store-address trigger set at 0x80008000 raised a breakpoint, but Whisper wrote 0x80008001 to mtval instead of the faulting address. I reported it, and after I sent the exact config and trace, the maintainer reproduced and fixed it.
Data triggers ignored load-reserved instructions. A data-match trigger fired on ordinary loads like ld, but not when lr.d loaded the same value. Spike took the breakpoint, but Whisper didn’t. I reported it with side-by-side traces from both simulators, and it was fixed.

title: Writing Certification Tests for RISC-V Sdtrig
text:
What I’ve Learned
Reference models disagree, and so do people reading the spec. Neither simulator is ground truth. While unifying the mcontrol6 tests, I found that Spike converts the negated match types to plain “equal.” That means Spike can’t serve as the reference for those match types, so those tests stay disabled until there’s a reference that can. Much of the work is deciding what the spec actually requires, then citing the rule when you file a bug.
A passing test might not be testing anything. In one case, the Sdtrig CSR access tests were guarded by #ifdef UDB_tdata1_AVAILABLE, but UDB defines the uppercase name UDB_TDATA1_AVAILABLE. No guard ever matched, so the access tests silently emitted no CSR accesses at all. Now I check that a test actually emits the instructions it claims to before I trust a green result.
Make bugs easy to reproduce. My first Whisper report included a trace from a different run than the ELF I attached, which cost the maintainer time. The simulator’s developers also don’t use the ACT build system, so a make target means nothing to them. Now every report I file includes the exact simulator command line, the config, and matching traces from both simulators.
Infrastructure is part of the job. Before I could verify my own tests, I had to repair the Whisper/Spike configs after a UDB schema change left them unable to build. Contributing to a large shared repository means fixing things that are broken for everyone, not just your own corner.
This work ties directly into my coursework. In System-on-Chip Design, I used the same ACT framework to verify the pipelined RISC-V processor my partner and I built.
